claims.claim: Requirements work can be understood as determining, documenting, and managing stakeholder needs and requirements in relation to project objectives.
Relevant stakeholder needs may include expectations, constraints, and interfaces; elicitation brings those inputs into a form that can be developed as requirements.
A project boundary or scope provides a framework for deciding whether a proposed requirement belongs to the effort, but scope is not itself a complete list of requirements.
Requirements documentation should express what is needed rather than prematurely commit to low-level solution design; the exact level of detail depends on context.
Validation examines whether requirements would enable the resulting product to perform appropriately in its intended-use environment; it is distinct from simply checking that a document exists.
A traceability record can connect detailed requirements to the business need and associated test scenarios, making the relationship available for review.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The sources describe requirements work in professional, IT, and systems-engineering contexts rather than one universal classroom process.
positions: PMI emphasizes scope boundaries, stakeholder involvement, and the distinction between needs and low-level design.
GAO reports selected project and systems-engineering practices such as elicitation, validation, and traceability.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson treats these as transferable analytical concepts. It does not prescribe a meeting format, approval chain, template, or organizational workflow.

unsupportedExistingClaims: A generated draft could confuse a stakeholder wish, a requirement, a scope boundary, and an acceptance criterion, or present a particular documentation format as mandatory.
correctionsNeeded: Uses original prose to distinguish the four related concepts and retains an explicit what-versus-how boundary.
Uses an original library example to show how a need becomes a candidate requirement with observable acceptance criteria.
Limits validation to checking fit with intended use rather than promising project success or prescribing organizational sign-off.
rightsIssues: PMI’s conference paper was read live and treated as REFERENCE_ONLY; no source prose, figures, or templates were reproduced.
GAO reports were read live and treated as public-domain U.S. government publications; the lesson uses original prose and reproduces no tables or diagrams.

questionKeyCheck.method: Read every saved prompt, all four options, correctIndex, explanation, and sourceIds after writing.
questionKeyCheck.result: Exactly five four-option questions. Keys span A through D, no position is used more than twice, and the bank includes recall, application, and analysis.

sourceRecords.title: Creating clear project requirements: differentiating what from how
sourceRecords.notes: Read live. Supports stakeholder involvement, a scope boundary before requirements definition, and the distinction between project needs and low-level design. An authored PMI conference paper, not a universal procedure; original prose only.

sourceRecords.title: Information Technology: Education Needs to Address Student Aid Modernization Weaknesses (GAO-23-105333)
sourceRecords.notes: Official GAO report checked live. Supports general descriptions of defining, validating, controlling, and tracking baseline requirements; used only for original synthesis.

sourceRecords.title: Air Traffic Control: System Management Capabilities Improved, but More Can Be Done to Institutionalize Improvements
sourceRecords.notes: Read live, especially pages 75–83. Supports the bounded systems example: elicit needs, expectations, constraints, and interfaces; translate them to customer requirements; analyze requirements for necessity and sufficiency; and validate intended-use performance using appropriate techniques. Original prose only; no federal procedure is presented as universal.
